This review maps AI applications against current clinical limitations, established benchmark tools, translational readiness, and equity-related implementation gaps. In detection, AI models integrate multimarker blood panels, routine laboratory indicators, ultrasound imaging, and cell-free DNA (cfDNA)-derived molecular signals to improve risk stratification beyond traditional biomarkers such as CA125, although prospective validation remains limited. In treatment and prognosis, pathology-based, radiomics-based, omics-based, and multimodal AI models show potential for predicting homologous recombination deficiency (HRD), platinum response, recurrence risk, and survival outcomes, but most remain retrospective or externally validated rather than clinically deployed. Blood/laboratory-based and ultrasound-assisted AI appear closest to workflow-based evaluation, whereas cfDNA-based screening, population-level AI detection, and multimodal prognostic models remain preliminary. Future efforts should prioritize prospective multicenter studies, benchmarked evaluation, transparent reporting, cost-effectiveness analysis, workflow integration, and globally representative datasets. Ultimately, AI should be judged by its ability to improve timely, affordable, and equitable OC care.

records.title: Technological Integration in Triage With AI and Machine Learning Compared With Conventional Triage and Narrative Synthesis of Telehealth for Patient Prioritization in Emergency and Acute Care Settings: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

content.title: Technological Integration in Triage With AI and Machine Learning Compared With Conventional Triage and Narrative Synthesis of Telehealth for Patient Prioritization in Emergency and Acute Care Settings: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Conventional triage relies on clinician judgment and limited information available at first contact. AI and machine learning (ML) may improve early risk stratification, whereas tele-triage and patient-facing tools primarily support remote assessment, access, and care routing.

Objective

This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic and prognostic performance of AI- and ML-assisted triage systems and summarize evidence on tele-triage, workflow, implementation, economic, and equity outcomes.

Methods

Comparative studies published between January 1, 2010, and December 31, 2025, evaluating AI-, ML-, natural language processing-, telehealth-, or digitally enhanced triage. At first, clinical contacts were included. PubMed/MEDLINE, CINAHL, Web of Science, Scopus, preprint servers, trial registries, and conference proceedings were searched. Screening and data extraction were performed independently in duplicate. Risk of bias was assessed using design-appropriate tools. Clinically comparable area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) estimates were synthesized using random-effects meta-analysis; heterogeneous diagnostic, operational, implementation, economic, and equity outcomes were summarized narratively. Exploratory scenario modeling projected effects per 10,000 emergency department (ED) visits.

Results

Twenty-seven studies were included, comprising 13 studies in the quantitative evidence stream and 14 in the narrative synthesis. Four adult ED studies evaluating critical care or deterioration outcomes demonstrated high pooled discrimination for AI-assisted triage (AUC 0.874; 95% CI 0.845-0.898; I²=94.4%; 95% prediction interval 0.803-0.922). Four studies reported directly extractable within-study comparisons favoring AI-assisted models (AUC differences of 0.097, 0.120, 0.108, and 0.065), although these could not be pooled because paired variance estimates were unavailable. Admission/disposition studies reported AI-model AUCs ranging from 0.80 to 0.93 and were summarized descriptively because extreme heterogeneity precluded meaningful pooling. Two pediatric studies (AUCs of 0.85-0.99) were summarized descriptively. Prediction-model studies were primarily limited by deficiencies in model analysis, calibration reporting, and external validation. Narrative evidence suggested improved front-door operational metrics with tele-triage, including reported reductions of 15%-40% in time to clinical assessment and 2-8 percentage points in left-without-being-seen rates, whereas patient-facing symptom checkers generally favored sensitivity over specificity. Exploratory scenario modeling illustrated that, under specified prevalence and threshold assumptions, AI-assisted triage could be associated with 12-38 fewer missed critical illness cases and 45-120 additional false-positive escalations per 10,000 ED visits. Economic and equity findings were assumption-dependent projections rather than observed clinical, cost-effectiveness, or equity outcomes.

Conclusions

AI- and ML-assisted triage models demonstrate promising discrimination for adult ED risk stratification; however, AUC-based discrimination does not establish superiority at clinically relevant decision thresholds, improved patient outcomes, or readiness for clinical implementation. Interpretation is limited by substantial heterogeneity, incomplete threshold-level performance and calibration reporting, limited external validation, and sparse pediatric evidence. Prospective multicenter validation, workflow assessment, subgroup calibration and equity auditing, and formal economic evaluation are required before routine implementation.

records.title: Effects of high-intensity interval training and moderate-intensity continuous training on body composition and glucose and lipid metabolism in college students: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Effects of high-intensity interval training and moderate-intensity continuous training on body composition and glucose and lipid metabolism in college students: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

This study systematically evaluated high-intensity interval training (HIIT) versus moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) for body composition and glucose and lipid metabolism markers in college students.

Methods

This PRISMA 2020-based systematic review searched PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Embase, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), and VIP Database (VIP) from inception to March 10, 2026. Restricted maximum likelihood (REML) random-effects models pooled mean differences (MDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran's Q and I2. Subgroup, meta-regression, sensitivity, publication bias, RoB 2.0, and GRADE analyses were conducted.

Results

A total of 20 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 745 college students were included, with 377 in HIIT and 368 in MICT. Compared with MICT, HIIT significantly reduced body weight (MD = -1.23 kg, 95% CI -1.94 to -0.52, P = 0.002), body fat percentage (MD = -1.21%, 95% CI -2.12 to -0.30, P = 0.013), waist-to-hip ratio (MD = -0.01, 95% CI -0.02 to -0.00, P = 0.014), waist circumference (MD = -1.33 cm, 95% CI -2.40 to -0.26, P = 0.023), and fat mass (MD = -0.99 kg, 95% CI -1.66 to -0.33, P = 0.010). No significant differences were found for body mass index (BMI), hip circumference, muscle mass, total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides (TG), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), fasting blood glucose (FBG), or fasting insulin (FINS). Subgroup analyses suggested sex might influence body weight and BMI effects, but most analyses showed no clear moderation. Meta-regression detected no significant moderation by duration or weekly HIIT volume. Evidence for body composition outcomes was mostly moderate, low, or very low; evidence for glucose and lipid metabolism outcomes was very low.

Conclusion

Compared with MICT, HIIT may provide greater benefits for selected body composition measures in college students, particularly body weight, body fat percentage, waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio, and fat mass. However, HIIT did not consistently improve routine glucose and lipid metabolism markers. Given the limited evidence quality, small number of studies, and uncertain moderator findings from subgroup and meta-regression analyses, larger randomized controlled trials with standardized protocols are needed.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, identifier CRD420261396573.

records.title: Artificial intelligence-driven assessment of sarcopenia in orthopedic geriatrics: technical progress and clinical implications.

content.title: Artificial intelligence-driven assessment of sarcopenia in orthopedic geriatrics: technical progress and clinical implications.
content.abstract: Sarcopenia, a progressive skeletal muscle disorder characterized by the loss of muscle mass and function, represents a significant challenge in geriatric orthopedics, with prevalence reaching as high as 48.7% in surgical populations. It is strongly associated with increased risks of falls, secondary fractures, postoperative complications, and mortality. Despite its clinical importance, traditional diagnostic methods like Dual-energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DXA) and Bioelectrical Impedance Analysis (BIA) are often impractical in acute orthopedic settings due to patient immobilization, positioning constraints, and postoperative fluid imbalances. This narrative review aims to summarize how the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning, addresses these gaps by enabling automated, high-throughput opportunistic screening from routine clinical imaging. Convolutional neural networks achieve expert-level segmentation of muscle quantity and quality, with Dice similarity coefficients often exceeding 0.94. AI-derived metrics serve as robust independent predictors for adverse surgical outcomes, including prolonged length of stay and infection, as well as functional recovery and one-year mortality. By integrating these metrics into Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS) and Electronic Medical Records (EMR), AI facilitates a paradigm shift from reactive fracture management to proactive prevention through automated "zero-click" alerts and multidisciplinary intervention pathways. While significant challenges regarding technical standardization, biological variability, and model interpretability persist, AI-driven assessment is transforming geriatric orthopedic care from subjective evaluation toward precise, objective quantification.

records.title: Artificial intelligence for early sepsis detection and dynamic prognostication in onco-critical care.
records.publisher: World journal of critical care medicine

content.title: Artificial intelligence for early sepsis detection and dynamic prognostication in onco-critical care.
content.abstract: Critically ill cancer patients have a unique physiological profile marked by severe immunosuppression, frailty, and multimorbidity, making traditional tools like Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II or Sequential Organ Failure Assessment often inadequate for accurate risk assessment. This review explores artificial intelligence's potential to transform onco-critical care from reactive to predictive management. We will synthesize literature on two key applications: Early sepsis detection in critically ill cancer patients and refining mortality prediction models to guide ethical care. The analysis will show how dynamic machine learning models, unlike static scores, use vital signs, lab trends, and unstructured machine learning data to detect deterioration hours before clinical decompensation. The review will also examine barriers to adoption, highlighting the need for explainable artificial intelligence to build clinician trust and address data heterogeneity across cancer populations. Ultimately, it will suggest that analytics can transform oncology intensive care unit care, balancing aggressive treatments and palliative care. While focusing on cancer patients, some evidence from general intensive care unit populations will be identified as extrapolated with caution, given different pathophysiology.

records.title: Rethinking bioinformatics expertise in the era of artificial intelligence.

content.title: Rethinking bioinformatics expertise in the era of artificial intelligence.
content.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is often framed as replacing scientific expertise, especially in bioinformatics. We argue instead that AI is a powerful accelerant whose value depends on expert guidance in design, data curation, interpretation, and governance. Because AI cannot judge biological meaning or verify scientific validity, bioinformaticians remain essential. Their role is shifting from workflow execution toward AI design, complex discovery, and responsible institutional leadership across research, translation, and clinical practice.

records.title: Incremental effects of SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and pioglitazone in type 2 diabetes and MASLD across Asian study settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Incremental effects of SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and pioglitazone in type 2 diabetes and MASLD across Asian study settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Objective

We evaluated the incremental hepatic and metabolic effects of adding sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), or pioglitazone to comparable background glucose-lowering therapy in Asian adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD).

Methods

We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science through 30 June 2026. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Eligible trials evaluated the addition of a study drug to background glucose-lowering management that was comparable between randomized groups and either remained stable or followed a prespecified adjustment protocol. Changes from baseline in alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) were coprimary outcomes. Secondary outcomes included aspartate aminotransferase, gamma-glutamyl transferase, magnetic resonance imaging-proton density fat fraction, liver stiffness, fibrosis-4 index, fasting plasma glucose, lipid parameters, body mass index, serum adiponectin, and systolic blood pressure. Random-effects pairwise meta-analyses were performed, and GRADE certainty was assessed for the two coprimary outcomes. Safety outcomes were synthesized narratively because reporting was heterogeneous and frequently incomplete.

Results

We included eleven randomized trials: 692 participants were randomized into eligible comparisons, of which 642 participated in the coprimary efficacy analyses. Moderate certainty was found for a reduction in ALT with the addition of an SGLT2 inhibitor compared with background therapy alone (mean difference [MD], - 7.56 U/L; 95% confidence interval [CI], - 11.24 to - 3.88); however, there was little or no clinically important further benefit observed for HbA1c (MD, - 0.09%; 95% CI, - 0.27 to 0.08; moderate certainty). Modest reductions in ALT were suggested by moderate certainty for GLP-1RAs (MD, - 6.71 U/L; 95% CI, - 11.53 to - 1.89) while low certainty indicated an HbA1c reduction (MD, - 0.48%; 95% CI, - 0.83 to - 0.14). Secondary exploratory findings favoring add-on therapy existed, although they are unadjusted for multiplicity. The comparative safety could not be assessed reliably.

Conclusion

In short-term randomized trials conducted in Asian study settings, adding SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1RAs may improve selected hepatic and metabolic surrogate outcomes. The available evidence does not support a treatment-class ranking, and the durability and clinical significance of these changes remain uncertain because follow-up was short and several comparisons were based on sparse evidence. Comparative safety also remains uncertain because adverse-event reporting was heterogeneous and incomplete.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, identifier CRD420251231137.

records.title: Regulation and Ethical Frameworks for AI in Health Professions Education: A Critical Narrative Review.
records.publisher: Journal of advances in medical education & professionalism

content.title: Regulation and Ethical Frameworks for AI in Health Professions Education: A Critical Narrative Review.
content.abstract:
Introduction

Integrating artificial intelligence (AI)-particularly generative AI and large language models (LLMs)-into health professions education offers substantial pedagogical opportunities, while highlighting critical gaps in existing ethical and regulatory frameworks. This critical narrative review examines how contemporary literature conceptualizes and addresses these challenges.

Methods

Publications from 2020-2025 were identified through searching PubMed, Scopus, and ERIC, focusing on AI, medical and health professions education, ethics, governance, and regulation. The initial search yielded 452 records; following two-stage screening (title/abstract and full-text review), thirty-four sources met the pre-defined inclusion criteria. These sources, including empirical studies, systematic reviews, policy documents, and conceptual papers, were included. Reflexive thematic analysis was used to synthesize the findings, while SANRA (Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles) informed the weighting of sources, which were categorized into high-, moderate-, and low-weight tiers.

Results

Four themes emerged: 1) a regulatory vacuum marked by policy lag and fragmented institutional responses; 2) reinterpretation of autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice in relation to opaque, datadriven systems, 3) generative AI's impact on scholarship, authorship, and academic integrity; and 4) equity, bias, and professional identity formation in AImediated learning environments. Integrating these themes with crosssector frameworks and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, the review develops a riskbased governance taxonomy for AI in Health Professions Education, distinguishing low, medium and highrisk educational use cases.

Conclusion

This synthesis indicates that current literature favors evolving beyond reactive policies. Consequently, we propose a theoretical shift toward risk-proportionate governance. We suggest that human-in-the-loop pedagogy should be prioritized as a conceptual framework to guide future research and policy development, rather than presenting it as a validated outcome.

records.title: The development and application of deep learning for stem cell research.
records.publisher: Journal of genetics and genomics = Yi chuan xue bao

content.title: The development and application of deep learning for stem cell research.
content.abstract: Stem cells reside in specific microenvironments where they divide to maintain themselves and differentiate into functional cells that replace old, dead, or damaged cells to maintain tissue homeostasis. Some stem cells could also be cultured in vitro for self-renewal and directed differentiation towards specific lineages for both mechanistic interrogation and clinical investigation. A deeper understanding of the regulatory mechanisms underlying stem cell properties is essential for advancing their translational applications. Deep learning (DL), a branch of artificial intelligence, has been widely and deeply incorporated into different fields including biology. The application of DL in stem cells has revolutionized our research strategies and provided significant technical advantages. Here, we review the latest advances of the application of DL in analyzing bioimaging data and exploring large-scale genomics data in stem cells. We also summarize the limitations of current DL models and challenges of the application of these models in stem cell research.

records.title: Emerging frontiers and challenges of artificial intelligence in PSMA-PET imaging: pioneering a new chapter in prostate cancer care.

content.title: Emerging frontiers and challenges of artificial intelligence in PSMA-PET imaging: pioneering a new chapter in prostate cancer care.
content.abstract: Prostate-specific membrane antigen positron emission tomography (PSMA-PET) has become pivotal in prostate cancer (PCa) management, offering superior sensitivity over conventional imaging for detecting tumors, metastases, and biochemical recurrence. However, interpretive subjectivity, workflow inefficiencies, and heterogeneous PSMA expression remain significant limitations. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly radiomics and deep learning, addresses these challenges by enabling automated lesion analysis and image enhancement. This review examines the impact of AI across the PSMA-PET workflow, covering optimized image acquisition (e.g., low-dose protocols, motion correction), enhanced interpretation (e.g., lesion characterization, prognostic stratification), and personalized theranostics (e.g., treatment response forecasting, radioligand therapy dosimetry). Despite promising multicenter validation, challenges remain in annotation standardization, data heterogeneity, model generalizability, interpretability, regulatory integration, and ethics. We further discuss emerging frontiers, including multimodal multi-omic integration, generative AI, and AI-driven clinical decision support systems. Notably, we highlight the evolving role of nuclear medicine physicians and radiologists as integrators of AI-derived biomarkers, who validate AI outputs for high-stakes decisions, retain interpretive authority for complex cases, and oversee quality assurance, ensuring that AI augments rather than replaces specialist expertise. These advances position AI-integrated PSMA-PET to drive precision oncology, with key pathways outlined for clinical translation and future innovation in PCa care.

records.title: The research hotspots and trends of artificial intelligence technology in nursing management: a bibliometric study.

content.title: The research hotspots and trends of artificial intelligence technology in nursing management: a bibliometric study.
content.abstract:
Background

Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in healthcare, with nursing management being a key area of application. As AI technologies such as machine learning and decision support systems are increasingly integrated into clinical workflows, understanding the research landscape of AI in nursing management becomes essential.

Methods

A total of 151 English-language publications from the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus (data from 1990 to August 2025) were analyzed using CiteSpace, VOSviewer, and Bibliometrix. Analyses included co-authorship networks, keyword co-occurrence, citation patterns, and trend visualizations.

Results

Since 2017, the number of relevant publications has surged, with China leading in output and the United States leading in collaborative centrality. Key institutions include Columbia University and Capital Medical University. Collaboration among authors remains limited, though several researchers exert significant influence. Five major research clusters have been identified, covering decision support, nursing leadership, informatics, behavioral aspects, and disease-specific applications. Emerging hotspots include "nursing management," "algorithms," and "deep learning."

Conclusion

In the field of nursing management, AI is transitioning from conceptual to practical application, demonstrating significant potential for enhancing decision-making and improving patient care. However, the field remains fragmented, with limited collaboration among authors and institutions. This study highlights AI's potential to transform nursing management while emphasizing the need for closer interdisciplinary and international cooperation. Future research should focus on addressing ethical concerns such as data privacy and transparency, and developing AI tools that integrate more effectively into nursing practice. While this study offers valuable insights, there are limitations, including the exclusion of non-English literature and reliance on bibliometric analysis, which may not fully reflect AI's real-world clinical applications. Looking ahead, fostering collaboration, improving ethical governance, and optimizing AI tools will be key to advancing AI in nursing management.

records.title: Medical Affairs in the Age of Complexity: From Scientific Support to Strategic Enterprise Integrator.

content.title: Medical Affairs in the Age of Complexity: From Scientific Support to Strategic Enterprise Integrator.
content.abstract: Regulatory acceleration, expanded reliance on real-world evidence (RWE), and increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare systems have substantially reshaped expectations placed on Medical Affairs. Accelerated and conditional approval pathways are progressively shifting confirmatory evidence generation into the post-marketing phase, while regulatory agencies have formalized frameworks for incorporating RWE into benefit-risk evaluation and lifecycle decision making. In parallel, healthcare systems are increasingly conceptualized as learning health systems in which routine-care data inform iterative improvement. This Leading Article proposes a conceptual but operationally applicable framework that positions Medical Affairs as a Strategic Enterprise Integrator, responsible for coordinating lifecycle evidence architecture, scientific exchange, insight translation, and governance across development and real-world settings. The framework is structured around four interdependent capability domains: lifecycle evidence architecture; scientific translation and insight management; cross-functional governance; and AI/data governance, including oversight of large language model (LLM)-supported workflows in medical information and analytics. The proposed model explicitly delineates interfaces with Clinical Development, Pharmacovigilance, Market Access/Health Economics and Outcomes Research, and Commercial functions to reduce redundancy while preserving functional accountability. Methodological considerations for RWE are anchored in principles of fit-for-purpose data, study design discipline, and transparent interpretation, while AI-enabled processes are addressed through a scientific governance lens emphasizing validation, auditability, and context-of-use. Illustrative operational examples and a staged maturity model with measurable indicators are introduced to support practical implementation. The framework positions Medical Affairs as a scientifically accountable integrator of lifecycle evidence within evolving regulatory science. As a conceptual model this framework requires further empirical validation to assess its applicability and generalizability across organizational contexts.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence (Pattern Recognition) in Musculoskeletal Imaging: The Future or Hype?

content.title: Artificial Intelligence (Pattern Recognition) in Musculoskeletal Imaging: The Future or Hype?
content.abstract:
Abstract

Artificial intelligence and automated pattern recognition, in particular, have been described as the next frontier in musculoskeletal imaging. However, as the initial hype phase transitions into clinical reality, an essential evaluation of these technologies is required. This narrative review examines the dichotomy between a potential future in which artificial intelligence offers unprecedented efficiency in automatizing multiple tasks in musculoskeletal radiology, from fracture detection, automated segmentation, to automated reporting, versus the hype, characterized by deep learning models that lack generalizability across different scanner vendors and patient populations. We explore the black box nature of deep learning and the ethical implications of automation. By analyzing current barriers to deployment, including workflow integration and regulatory hurdles, this article argues that although artificial intelligence holds transformative potential for musculoskeletal radiology, its success depends on moving beyond narrow diagnostic tasks toward robust multi-institutional validation, to evolve from a speculative trend into an essential clinical copilot tool.

records.title: Serum anti-Müllerian hormone levels in women following bariatric surgery: insights from a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Serum anti-Müllerian hormone levels in women following bariatric surgery: insights from a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Aim

This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effects of bariatric surgery on serum anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) levels in women, highlighting potential implications for ovarian reserve and fertility management.

Methods

A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and Embase databases up to February 2025. The included studies were observational in design (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional) and provided quantitative pre- and post-operative AMH data. Quality assessment was performed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, and data were analyzed using a random-effects meta-analysis.

Results

A total of 14 studies were included in the systematic review, with 591 participants contributing to the quantitative meta-analysis. The pooled results indicated that bariatric surgery did not significantly alter AMH levels overall (WMD = 0.05 ng/mL; 95% CI: -0.66, 0.75; p = 0.897), with substantial heterogeneity among effect estimates (I² = 93.9%, p < 0.001). Subgroup analyses suggested significant AMH reductions in studies with baseline AMH > 3 ng/mL, upper age limit ≤ 35 years, longer follow-up, retrospective design, smaller sample size, and South Asian populations, while a significant increase was observed in the fertile subgroup.

Conclusions

Bariatric surgery was not associated with a significant overall change in serum AMH levels. Findings suggest variable AMH responses across clinical and methodological contexts; however, given substantial heterogeneity and limited reproductive outcome data, these changes should be interpreted as dynamic endocrine biomarker responses rather than direct evidence of altered ovarian reserve or fertility potential.

Clinical trial number

Not applicable.

records.title: Efficacy and safety of fluoroquinolones in the treatment of human brucellosis: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Efficacy and safety of fluoroquinolones in the treatment of human brucellosis: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Introduction

Brucellosis is a major zoonotic infection worldwide, with the highest burden reported in the Mediterranean region. The therapeutic role of fluoroquinolones in this disease continues to be controversial. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of fluoroquinolone-containing regimens compared with standard non-fluoroquinolone regimens for the treatment of human brucellosis.

Methods

In accordance with PRISMA recommendations, this systematic review and meta-analysis assessed the efficacy and safety of fluoroquinolone-based regimens for treating brucellosis. It was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251142019). A comprehensive search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library was carried out, including studies published through August 2025. Randomized controlled trials comparing fluoroquinolones with conventional therapies (such as doxycycline with streptomycin or rifampicin) were included. Therapeutic failure, relapse, adverse events, and time to defervescence were the main outcomes. To compute pooled risk ratios and mean differences with 95%CIs, data were analyzed using STATA v18. The GRADE method and the RoB 2 tool were used to evaluate the risk of bias and the certainty of the evidence.

Results

The analysis comprised 9 clinical studies with 602 brucellosis patients. When compared to standard regimens, fluoroquinolone-based regimens were linked to a significantly higher risk of therapeutic failure (RR = 2.11, 95% CI: 1.26-3.51; P = 0.004) and a higher, though not statistically significant, risk of relapse (RR = 1.88, 95% CI: 0.94-3.74; P = 0.07). No statistically significant between-study heterogeneity was observed for either outcome (I² = 0%). Subgroup analyses showed a significantly increased risk of therapeutic failure in patients with uncomplicated brucellosis and in studies with treatment durations >8 weeks, although between-subgroup differences were not statistically significant. On the other hand, no statistically significant difference in adverse events was observed between fluoroquinolone-based and standard regimens under the random-effects model (RR = 0.62, 95% CI: 0.29-1.33; P = 0.22). Although the point estimate favored fluoroquinolone-based regimens, the confidence interval included the null effect. Fluoroquinolone-based regimens were also associated with a significantly longer time to defervescence compared with standard regimens (MD = 1.20 days, 95% CI: 0.66-1.74; P < 0.001). The certainty of evidence was moderate for therapeutic failure, and time to defervescence, and low for relapse and adverse events according to the GRADE evaluation.

Conclusion

Compared with conventional doxycycline-based combinations, fluoroquinolone-based regimens were associated with a higher risk of therapeutic failure and longer time to defervescence, while the overall risk of relapse did not differ significantly. No significant difference in adverse events was observed with the random-effects model, although the point estimate favored fluoroquinolone-based regimens. Overall, these findings do not support the routine use of fluoroquinolones as first-line therapy for adult brucellosis. Further well-designed randomized controlled trials are needed.

records.title: A dual-level Bayesian network meta-analysis of first-line immunotherapy in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma: strategy-level and regimen-level evidence.

content.title: A dual-level Bayesian network meta-analysis of first-line immunotherapy in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma: strategy-level and regimen-level evidence.
content.abstract:
Background

Phase III trials of first-line immunotherapy-based combinations for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) have yielded heterogeneous results, and head-to-head comparisons remain scarce. We evaluated mechanism-based strategy classes and individual regimens using a dual-level Bayesian network meta-analysis to provide a structured interpretation of the current evidence.

Methods

We systematically searched the literature up to December 28, 2025, and identified 15 phase III randomised controlled trials. A dual-level Bayesian network meta-analysis was performed using separate models at the strategy level (PD-(L)1 plus VEGF monoclonal antibody (VEGF(Ab)), PD-(L)1 plus tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), PD-(L)1 plus CTLA-4, and PD-(L)1 monotherapy) and the regimen level. Outcomes included overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), objective response rate (ORR), and grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs).

Results

Fifteen trials comprising 9,792 patients were included. At the strategy level, PD-(L)1 plus VEGF(Ab) showed the most favourable OS effect versus TKI monotherapy and the highest efficacy-oriented ranking, followed by PD-(L)1 plus CTLA-4 and PD-(L)1 plus TKI. PD-(L)1 plus TKI also improved PFS but was associated with a higher toxicity and discontinuation burden, whereas PD-(L)1 monotherapy showed the most favourable tolerability profile. At the regimen level, atezolizumab plus bevacizumab, sintilimab plus IBI305, camrelizumab plus rivoceranib, and STRIDE showed OS benefit versus sorafenib.

Conclusions

In this evidence network, PD-(L)1 plus VEGF(Ab) showed the most efficacy-oriented profile and was supported by relatively consistent regimen-level estimates. However, the clinical interpretation of strategy-level findings differed across classes: PD-(L)1 plus TKI required closer regimen-level assessment because of greater within-class variability and a less favourable toxicity profile, whereas PD-(L)1 plus CTLA-4 and PD-(L)1 monotherapy showed distinct benefit-risk patterns. This dual-level framework complements regimen-centric evidence by distinguishing strategy-level patterns from regimen-level findings and by supporting a structured interpretation of efficacy-toxicity trade-offs in first-line ICI-based therapy for advanced HCC.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251273309, identifier CRD420251273309.

records.title: Shifting from black box decisions to informed decision-making in using artificial intelligence to analyze prostate MRI.

content.title: Shifting from black box decisions to informed decision-making in using artificial intelligence to analyze prostate MRI.
content.abstract: Prostate magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is central to the detection and localization of clinically significant prostate cancers. However, its interpretation is time-consuming and variable. Artificial intelligence (AI) tools for prostate MRI are rapidly emerging, with their performance approaching that of expert readers in select settings, although robust external validation in unselected real-world cohorts remains incomplete. Moreover, many deep learning models are limited in terms of transparency; that is, the "black box" problem hinders trust, safe deployment, and regulatory acceptance. This review summarizes the core concepts of interpretability and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), highlights commonly used approaches to explain the output of AI models, and discusses how the lack of transparency hinders clinical deployment and how this can be addressed using standardized reporting frameworks. Ultimately, the purpose of this review is to draw attention to the pressing need for XAI and to spark interest and awareness of how standardized frameworks may help us to shift from "black box" decisions to informed decision-making in clinical practice.

records.title: Dumbbell Bench Press and Dumbbell Fly Elicit Similar Pectoralis Major Muscle Hypertrophy in Recreationally Trained Men.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Dumbbell Bench Press and Dumbbell Fly Elicit Similar Pectoralis Major Muscle Hypertrophy in Recreationally Trained Men.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Dell'Avanzi, FG, Enes, A, Alves-Marques, F, Costa-Rodrigues, J, Bello, G, Seima, G, Nass, G, Moreira, NF, Santana, C, Mohan, AE, Piñero, A, Schoenfeld, BJ, and Souza-Junior, TP. Dumbbell bench press and dumbbell fly elicit similar pectoralis major muscle hypertrophy in recreationally trained men. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Exercise selection is one of the main resistance training (RT) variables for eliciting inhomogeneous muscle growth. Whether exercises that differ in resistance moment arm elicit whole- and nonuniform hypertrophy of the pectoralis major remains unclear. This study investigated the effects of the dumbbell bench press (DBP) and dumbbell fly (DFLY) on pectoralis major muscle thickness (MT). Twenty-six young healthy men (RT experience 3.3 ± 3.1 years) were allocated to DBP or DFLY groups, training twice a week over a 10-week period. The weekly set number was individualized according to subjects' previous RT pectoralis major volume. Pectoralis major MT was assessed by ultrasound imaging at medial (30%), intermediate (50%), and lateral (70%) sites at baseline and postintervention. Our mixed-model analysis indicated a main effect for time (p < 0.05) but no time-by-group interaction for the medial site (p = 0.500), intermediate site (p = 0.864), lateral site (p = 0.720), and the sum of the MT across sites (p = 0.985). Therefore, both exercises elicited similar general and regional hypertrophy on pectoralis major MT in recreationally trained individuals. Coaches and practitioners can select DBP or DFLY when targeting pectoralis major muscle development in recreationally trained men based on personal preference and goals within the RT program.

records.title: Is plant-based protein supplementation as effective as whey protein? A systematic review and meta-analysis in untrained adults undergoing resistance training.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Is plant-based protein supplementation as effective as whey protein? A systematic review and meta-analysis in untrained adults undergoing resistance training.
content.abstract:
Background

Dietary protein supplements are commonly consumed to support increases in lean body mass among healthy adults engaged in resistance training (RT). Although whey protein has been extensively investigated, plant-based protein supplements have emerged as a viable alternative for individuals who avoid animal-derived products.

Methods

The present study aims to evaluate, through a systematic review and meta-analysis, the effects of plant-based versus whey protein supplementation on body composition in untrained adults (18-59 years) undergoing RT, using Dual-Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry (DEXA). The systematic review was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 checklist and was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251145410). Searches were conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect, identifying 5 studies that met the inclusion criteria for qualitative synthesis and meta-analysis.

Results

When combined with RT, both plant-based and whey protein supplementation were associated with improvements in lean body mass (LBM) and body fat mass (BFM), with no significant between-group differences observed.

Conclusions

Thus, soy- and pea-based protein supplements may support favorable body composition changes in adults initiating RT and could be considered practical nutritional options for individuals seeking alternatives to whey protein. Regarding chia-based protein, the available evidence is currently limited to a single study that did not demonstrate significant changes in lean body mass; therefore, firm conclusions regarding its efficacy cannot be drawn at this time.

records.title: How Often Should Volume Increase? Effects of Different Volume-Progression Frequencies on Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations in Women.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: How Often Should Volume Increase? Effects of Different Volume-Progression Frequencies on Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations in Women.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Enes, A, Macedo, ACG, Nass, G, Costa-Rodrigues, J, Alves-Marques, F, Santana, C, Dell'Avanzi, FG, Rodrigues, BG, Alves, RC, De Souza, EO, and Souza-Junior, TP. How often should volume increase? Effects of different volume-progression frequencies on strength and hypertrophy adaptations in females. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Resistance training (RT) volume is an important programming variable for strength and hypertrophy. However, how frequently RT volume should be progressed remains unclear. Thus, we investigated the effects of progressively increasing RT volume by 2 weekly sets targeting the quadriceps femoris every 2 weeks (2 W) or every 4 weeks (4 W) over a 12-week period in recreationally trained women. Using a within-subject design and accounting for previous RT volume, 21 subjects (age 23.3 ± 3.9 years; RT experience 1.1 ± 0.7 years) had their limbs assigned to one of the 2 conditions: 2 weeks (2 W) or 4 weeks (4 W). 45° leg-press 1-repetition maximum (1RM) and the sum of muscle thickness (∑MT) of the proximal (30%), middle (50%), and distal (70%) portions of the lateral thigh were assessed at baseline and after 12 weeks. Our mixed-model analysis indicated a main effect of time for 1RM (p < 0.0001), with no difference between the 2 and 4 W conditions (p = 0.317). Similarly, regarding the ∑MT, the analysis indicated a main effect of time (p < 0.001), with no difference between the conditions (p = 0.616). Within the relatively high training volumes examined, progressing the RT volume by 2 weekly sets every 2 or 4 weeks did not elicit detectable differences in strength and hypertrophy adaptations over 12 weeks in recreationally trained women.

records.title: Lower-Body Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations in Response to Concurrent Training in Trained Young Males.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Lower-Body Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations in Response to Concurrent Training in Trained Young Males.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Gomes, M, Costa, M, Pezarat-Correia, P, and Mendonca, GV. Lower-body strength and hypertrophy adaptations in response to concurrent training in trained young males. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study examined the interference effect of concurrent training (CT) on maximal and explosive strength and muscle morphology in trained young males. Thirty subjects were randomly assigned to endurance training (E), resistance training (R), or CT for 11 weeks. The intervention comprised 2 mesocycles: weeks 1-5 emphasizing maximal strength, and weeks 6-11 targeting explosive strength. Assessments were conducted at baseline, mid-training, and post-training, and included leg-press maximal voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC), rate of force development (RFD), countermovement jump kinetics, and vastus lateralis cross-sectional area and pennation angle. Maximal voluntary isometric contraction increased only in the R group (18.4 ± 10.2%, p = 0.015). Peak RFD improved in both R (31.8 ± 23.2%) and CT (23.1 ± 27.9%), although with distinct time courses: R improved progressively across both mesocycles, whereas CT improved only during the second. Early-phase RFD (0-50 ms) increased in the R group from mid-training onward, whereas the CT group improved only from mid- to post-training (38.3 ± 40.4%, p = 0.021), accompanied by greater quadriceps electromyographic activity (p < 0.05). No changes in RFD were observed in E during training. Countermovement jump positive impulse improved in both R (12.7 ± 9.0%) and CT (8.8 ± 8.3%, p < 0.05), with no evidence of interference in jump-related explosive performance. Cross-sectional area increased in both R (17.0 ± 13.0%) and CT (8.8 ± 9.4%, p < 0.05). Pennation angle increased in CT (10.1 ± 12.9%) and R (18.6 ± 15.1%). These findings indicate that, although CT may limit MVIC development and delay early-phase RFD adaptations, it does not hinder explosive performance when resistance training is oriented toward rapid-strength development. Thus, CT can be effectively implemented in trained individuals when resistance training is periodized to emphasize neural-driven explosive or hypertrophy-related adaptations.

records.title: Effects of In-Season Contrast Strength Training on Jump Performance and Sprint Ability in Female Field Hockey Players.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Effects of In-Season Contrast Strength Training on Jump Performance and Sprint Ability in Female Field Hockey Players.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Chilingirian-Padrón, R, Álvarez-Yates, T, and García-García, O. Effects of in-season contrast strength training on jump performance and sprint ability in female field hockey players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The purpose of this study was to examine the effects of a 6-week in-season contrast strength training program incorporating sport-specific tasks on neuromuscular performance in sub-elite female field hockey players. Twenty-five athletes completed a pre-post single-cohort intervention integrated into their regular team schedule. Each session consisted of 3 sequential blocks: (a) a high-load strength exercise targeting maximal strength or hypertrophy (70-85% 1 repetition maximum [1RM]); (b) a biomechanically related explosive action performed at low load (∼30% 1RM) and high execution velocity; and (c) a high-speed sport-specific task. Jump performance was assessed using bilateral and unilateral countermovement jumps (CMJs) and free arm CMJ, whereas sprint ability was evaluated through 10- and 20-m sprints. A mixed-model repeated-measures analysis of variance was used to determine the effects of the intervention, with Time (Pre, Post) as within-subject factor and Playing Position (defenders, midfielders, forwards) as between-subject factor, with the level of significance set at p ≤ 0.05. Significant improvements were observed in all jump and sprint assessments: jump performance increased by 5.7-29.6%, whereas sprint ability improved by 1.6-1.9%. These findings indicate that 6 weeks of contrast strength training incorporating high-speed sports-specific tasks performed during the competitive season elicited meaningful improvements in stretch-shortening cycle-related jump performance and sprint ability in sub-elite female field hockey players.

records.title: Comparison of Functional and Traditional Strength and Power Training on U19 Soccer Players During Offseason in Norway: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Comparison of Functional and Traditional Strength and Power Training on U19 Soccer Players During Offseason in Norway: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Engberg Treu Lassen, L, Kersting, UG, and Pessoto Hirata, R. Comparison of functional and traditional strength and power training on U19 soccer players during off-season in Norway: A randomized controlled trial. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Functional training emphasizes multiplanar, soccer-specific movement patterns requiring body control, whereas traditional resistance training focuses on maximal force production through stable, bilateral lifts. Although both approaches are common in soccer physical preparation, their relative effects on soccer-specific performance remain uncertain. This study compared the effects of functional vs. traditional strength training on performance outcomes during the offseason in U19 male players. Thirty-three Norwegian players were randomly allocated to a functional training group (FTG, n = 11), a traditional training group (TTG, n = 11), or a control group (CG, n = 11) using stratified, concealed allocation. During the first 4 weeks, all groups completed 2 weekly soccer sessions; FTG and TTG additionally completed 2 supervised 70-minute strength sessions per week. In the final 4 weeks, FTG and TTG continued the twice-weekly strength training, whereas CG ceased organized training. Functional training group performed unilateral, multiplanar free-weight exercises, while TTG performed bilateral, uniplanar machine-based exercises. The primary outcome was technical soccer performance, with mobility, dynamic balance, sprint speed, change of direction, and vertical jump as secondary outcomes. Both FTG and TTG improved Loughborough Soccer Shooting Test (LSST) performance compared with CG (FTG: -0.43 seconds, p = 0.003, d = 1.62; TTG: -0.50 seconds, p < 0.001, d = 1.88). Traditional training group also increased body mass compared with the CG (2.20 kg, p = 0.002, d = 1.65). Functional and traditional strength training produced comparable improvements in LSST time. These findings highlight training dose response and support individualized off-season programs integrating physical preparation with sport-specific demands.

records.title: Effectiveness of Pelvic Floor Muscle Training in Women Soccer Players and Its Relationship With Quality of Life and Pelvic Floor Muscle Strength: A Randomized Controlled Pilot Study.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Effectiveness of Pelvic Floor Muscle Training in Women Soccer Players and Its Relationship With Quality of Life and Pelvic Floor Muscle Strength: A Randomized Controlled Pilot Study.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Sebastian-Rico, JM, Muñoz-Fernández, MJ, Martínez-Aranda, LM, Calvo-Lluch, Á, and Ortega-Becerra, M. Effectiveness of pelvic floor muscle training in women soccer players and its relationship with quality of life and pelvic floor muscle strength: a randomized controlled pilot study. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study investigated the effects of a 6-week pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) program on muscle strength, function, and the prevalence of related dysfunctions in professional female soccer players using a randomized controlled pilot study design. Twenty nulliparous professional soccer players from the Spanish professional league (2024-2025 season) were randomly assigned to an experimental group (n = 12) or a control group (n = 8). Assessments included anthropometric data, validated questionnaires (International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire-Short Form and Broome Pelvic Muscle Self-Efficacy Scale), clinical interviews, and physical examination using the PERFECT method and manometry. The intervention consisted of a 6-week supervised PFMT program (4 sessions/week, 30 minutes each) progressed through 4 phases: education, proprioception, strengthening, and functional integration. Results showed significant group × time interactions for pelvic floor self-efficacy (Broome Pelvic Muscle Self-Efficacy Scale), with scores in the PFMT group increasing by 48.8 and 59.6% (p < 0.05), representing large between-group effect sizes (d = 0.91-1.26). Pelvic floor muscle performance increased by 122.4% in the intervention group (d = 1.25), whereas no meaningful changes were observed in the control group. No adverse events were reported. In conclusion, a 6-week supervised PFMT program is an effective and safe intervention for professional female soccer players, significantly improving muscle function and self-efficacy. These findings support the integration of PFMT for both therapeutic and preventive purposes in elite, high-impact sports environments.

records.title: Performance and Physiological Responses to Strength Training Programs in Elite Judo Athletes.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Performance and Physiological Responses to Strength Training Programs in Elite Judo Athletes.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Campos, BT, Rodrigues, JGdS, Cal Abad, CC, Bachi, ALL, dos Santos, CMM, Tritto, AC, Kons, RL, Penna, EM, and Prado, LS. Performance and physiological responses to strength training programs in elite judo athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study compared the effects of 2 short-term strength training models, block planning (BP) and undulating planning (UP), on performance, physiological, and perceptual responses in elite judo athletes. We hypothesized that BP would induce greater physiological strain due to the concentration of training stimuli. Eighteen judokas (14 men and 4 women) were randomly assigned to BP (n = 9) or UP (n = 9) for 4 weeks, performing 6 weekly strength sessions alongside technical-tactical training. Performance outcomes included countermovement jump (CMJ), muscle power (back squat and bent-over row), and the Special Judo Fitness Test (SJFT). Monitoring variables included internal load, heart rate variability (HRV), and well-being, while physiological markers included creatine kinase, tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and cortisol. Data were analyzed using 2-way repeated-measures ANOVA (p < 0.05). Both groups improved SJFT performance (p < 0.01), with no between-group differences. Block planning increased lower-limb peak power (p = 0.01; d = 0.90), whereas UP showed no meaningful change. Upper-limb power and CMJ did not change in either group. Internal load showed different temporal patterns between models. Block planning presented higher HRVcv values (p = 0.04), indicating greater autonomic perturbation. Creatine kinase and TNF-α increased over time in both groups (p ≤ 0.05), while cortisol showed an interaction without clear post hoc differences. In conclusion, BP improved lower-limb power but increased physiological strain, whereas UP elicited similar judo-specific improvements with lower recovery demands. These findings highlight the importance of training organization for balancing performance and recovery in elite judo athletes.

records.title: Low-Intensity Resistance Training Improves Irisin-Associated Endothelial Function in Aging.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Low-Intensity Resistance Training Improves Irisin-Associated Endothelial Function in Aging.
content.abstract:
Purpose

Low-intensity resistance training (LRT) may be suitable for both muscle and cardiovascular health of older adults. However, its effects and mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to examine whether LRT improves endothelial function in adult senescence-accelerated mouse prone 1 (SAMP1) mice, a model of accelerated aging, and whether this response is accompanied by changes in circulating irisin, arterial protein kinase B (Akt)/endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) signaling, and nitric oxide (NO) levels.

Methods

Adult (38-week-old) SAMP1 mice were randomized to three groups: LRT (climbing a ladder at 40% maximal carrying capacity, 3 days/week for 12 weeks), high-intensity resistance training (80%), or sedentary control, with assessment at 50 weeks of age. Young (13-week-old) SAMP1 mice were used as a sedentary-control group. In the human study, 17 healthy middle-aged and older adults were allocated to an LRT or control group in a randomized controlled trial. LRT participants performed an elastic band-based resistance training program for 45 min, three times per week, for 8 weeks.

Results

In adult mice, aging was associated with reduced circulating irisin levels and muscle fibronectin type III domain-containing protein 5 (FNDC5) expression, accompanied by impaired endothelial function, diminished arterial NO production, and attenuated Akt/eNOS signaling. These age-related impairments were improved by LRT. Consistent with these findings in mice, LRT in middle-aged and older adults increased circulating nitrate/nitrite (NOx) and irisin concentrations, accompanied by improvements in endothelial function.

Conclusions

These findings suggest that LRT-induced enhancement of circulating irisin secretion in adult SAMP1 mice and middle-aged and older adults may be involved in the improvement of endothelial function accompanied by increased NO production and the activation of the arterial Akt/eNOS signaling pathway.

records.title: The effects of a 4-week protein overfeeding protocol on body composition and influence of FTO genotype in exercise-trained men and women.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: The effects of a 4-week protein overfeeding protocol on body composition and influence of FTO genotype in exercise-trained men and women.
content.abstract:
Background

High-protein diets have consistently been associated with favorable changes in body composition in both sedentary and exercise-trained populations. Despite abundant evidence supporting protein intakes above the recommended dietary allowance (RDA) for active individuals, the effects of deliberate protein overfeeding, particularly in those already consuming adequate protein, remain incompletely characterized. The primary purpose of this study was to examine the effects of a 4-week protein overfeeding protocol on body composition in exercise-trained men and women. The secondary purpose was to determine whether body composition adaptations differed by FTO rs9939609 genotype.

Methods

Fifty-six exercise-trained men and women (age: 22.40 ± 5.78 years; body mass: 75.47 ± 14.98 kg; BMI: 24.52 ± 3.50 kg/m2; resistance training: 5.12 ± 3.35 h/week) were enrolled in a 4-week dietary intervention. Participants were instructed to increase their daily protein intake by approximately 20% above baseline while maintaining habitual training. Body composition was assessed pre- and post-intervention using a multi-frequency bioelectrical impedance device (InBody® 270). Dietary intake was self-monitored via MyFitnessPal®. Thirty-five participants completed both pre- and post-testing assessments and constituted the primary analysis. Linear regression models adjusted for baseline values indicated that FTO genotype was not a significant predictor of body composition changes (p > 0.05).

Results

Protein intake trended toward a significant increase over the 4-week period (pre: 146 ± 66 g/day vs. post: 164 ± 79 g/day; p = 0.053), representing an approximate 12% increase. Total energy intake, carbohydrate, and fat intake did not significantly change. Lean body mass increased significantly (pre: 59.95 ± 14.14 kg vs. post: 60.62 ± 14.42 kg; p = 0.005; Cohen's d = 0.31) and total body water increased significantly (pre: 43.85 ± 10.35 L vs. post: 44.34 ± 10.55 L; p = 0.005). Fat mass (p = 0.424), body fat percentage (p = 0.149), and total body mass (p = 0.09) did not significantly change.

Conclusions

A 4-week modest protein overfeeding protocol in exercise-trained men and women was associated with a significant increase in lean body mass and total body water without concomitant increases in fat mass. These adaptations were not modified by FTO rs9939609 genotype. These findings support the contention that higher protein intakes do not promote fat accretion and may facilitate improvements in body composition in trained individuals.

records.title: Do Putative Human Reticulospinal Tract Properties Adapt Following Short-Term Isometric Resistance Training?
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Do Putative Human Reticulospinal Tract Properties Adapt Following Short-Term Isometric Resistance Training?
content.abstract:
Purpose

The primary purpose of this study was to investigate whether isometric resistance training (RT) leads to reticulospinal tract (RST) adaptations.

Methods

A "RT group" of 30 healthy adults completed 4 weeks (15 sessions) of volume-matched unilateral elbow flexion RT involving high (32 repetitions/session at 70% maximal voluntary torque [MVT]) or low (64 repetitions/session at 35%MVT) loads. An additional 15 participants served as controls (CON group). Pre- and post-test MVT, RST properties (RST gain ratio derived from the StartReact assessment; startling auditory stimulus-conditioned/control motor evoked potential [MEP] ratio; and startling stimulus-conditioned/control cervicomedullary MEP [CMEP] ratio), CST excitability and intracortical inhibition properties (in response to transcranial magnetic stimulation) were assessed.

Results

MVT increased more in the RT group (+12.8%; n = 30) vs. CON group (-4.3%; n = 15; group (2) × time (2), p = 0.001). However, changes in RST properties assessed using a series of indirect measures did not differ between the RT group (-1.4% to 6.6%; n = 30) and CON group (-4.5% to 10.5%; n = 15; group (2) × time (2), 0.352 ≤ p ≤ 0.834).

Conclusions

RST adaptations within a sample of healthy young men and women, assessed using various indirect measurement approaches, did not occur following only 4 weeks of isometric elbow flexion RT. These findings add to the currently limited scientific evidence from short-term human RT intervention studies available to inform the use of RT for healthy individuals or patients primarily targeting the development of RST function.

records.title: Beyond the Hangover: Associations Between Binge Drinking, Health, and Performance in Young Adult Resistance-Trained Females.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Beyond the Hangover: Associations Between Binge Drinking, Health, and Performance in Young Adult Resistance-Trained Females.
content.abstract:
Purpose

The present study aimed to evaluate associations between resistance training and binge drinking in relation to musculoskeletal composition, physical fitness, cognitive function, and psychological wellness in young adult females.

Methods

Participants were categorized into four groups: sedentary low alcohol consumers (SL; n=12), sedentary binge drinkers (SB; n=12), resistance-trained low alcohol consumers (RTL; n=12), and resistance-trained binge drinkers (RTB; n=12). Measurements included body composition via DEXA scan, muscle quality via ultrasonography, and insulin sensitivity via oral glucose tolerance test. Physical performance was assessed using maximum chair stand power, vertical jump, broad jump, knee extensor torque, grip strength, and push-ups to failure. Tests and questionnaires were used to assess cognitive function and psychological wellness.

Results

Resistance-trained females had lower body fat than sedentary females (RTL = 29.28±4.27%; RTB = 29.03±3.67%; SL = 37.18±5.32%; SB = 34.83±3.54%; p<0.05), and RTL had more fat-free mass than SL and SB (RTL = 48.31±5.81 kg; SL = 38.08±6.59 kg; SB = 40.37±6.05 kg; both p<0.05). There were no differences between RTL and RTB in bone mineral density, muscle quality, or physical performance. RTL outperformed SL and SB on vertical jump (both p<0.05) while RTB outperformed SL and SB on broad jump. RTL had lower fasting blood glucose than RTB (88.92±12.09 mg/dL and 103.17 ± 10.21 mg/dL, respectively; p=0.008), and lower postprandial blood glucose than all groups (RTL = 103.83±19.82 mg/dL; RTB = 137.58±21.54 mg/dL; SL = 148.50±44.60 mg/dL; SB = 139.25±14.49 mg/dL; all p<0.05).

Conclusions

The results suggest that ≥1 year of binge drinking is associated with poorer metabolic health without differences in performance in young females. Further, frequent RT may mitigate the effects of binge drinking on body composition.

records.title: Exploratory serum renal biomarker and eGFR responses to high-protein diets during resistance versus concurrent training in resistance-trained men.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Exploratory serum renal biomarker and eGFR responses to high-protein diets during resistance versus concurrent training in resistance-trained men.
content.abstract:
Background

High protein intake is common among resistance-trained athletes, but its association with renal biomarkers across different exercise modalities remains uncertain. This study investigated whether consuming a high-protein diet (3.2 g·kg⁻¹·d⁻¹) during 16 weeks of resistance training (RT) or concurrent training (CT) affects renal biomarkers and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in resistance-trained men.

Methods

Forty-eight resistance-trained men (26 ± 6 years; BMI 25.6 ± 2.9 kg·m⁻²) were randomized to 16 weeks of RT or CT (4 sessions·wk⁻¹) while consuming either 1.6 or 3.2 g·kg⁻¹·d⁻¹ of protein in a 2 × 2 factorial design. Forty-four participants with complete pre- and post-intervention data were analyzed. Fasting blood samples were assessed for blood urea nitrogen (BUN), BUN/creatinine ratio, cystatin C, and eGFR calculated using the CKD-EPI creatinine (2021), cystatin C (2012), and creatinine-cystatin C (2021) equations. Within-group changes were evaluated using paired t-tests, and factorial effects were assessed using linear mixed-effects models (Time × Training × Protein).

Results

No statistically significant Time × Protein or Time × Training × Protein interactions were detected for any renal biomarker or eGFR estimate (all p ≥ 0.182). No significant within-group changes occurred in the 1.6 g·kg⁻¹·d⁻¹ groups (all p > 0.05). In both 3.2 g·kg⁻¹·d⁻¹ groups, BUN and cystatin C increased (all p ≤ 0.017), while eGFR estimates decreased (all p ≤ 0.009). The BUN/creatinine ratio remained unchanged (p ≥ 0.614). However, these within-group findings were descriptive because the corresponding interaction effects were not statistically significant.

Conclusions

In resistance-trained men, 16 weeks of high protein intake did not produce statistically detectable differences in renal biomarker or eGFR changes compared with moderate protein intake, irrespective of training modality. Although modest increases in BUN and cystatin C and small decreases in eGFR estimates were observed within the high-protein groups, these findings were not supported by significant factorial interactions. The limited sample size precludes excluding clinically meaningful differences, warranting further investigation in larger studies.

records.title: Multiple Sessions of Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation Combined With Squat Training Improve Lower-Limb Maximum Strength in Healthy Adult Men.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Multiple Sessions of Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation Combined With Squat Training Improve Lower-Limb Maximum Strength in Healthy Adult Men.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Yan, X, Zuo, Z, Nitsche, MA, Zhang, X, and Qi, F. Multiple sessions of transcranial direct current stimulation combined with squat training improve lower-limb maximum strength in healthy adult men. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study aimed to investigate the effects of transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) combined with Squat training (ST) on lower-limb maximum strength in healthy adult men. Sixty men (age: 21.6 ± 2.1 years, height: 177.5 ± 5.3 cm, body mass: 73.1 ± 7.4 kg) were randomly assigned to 4 groups (tDCS + ST group, sham tDCS + ST group, tDCS + rest group, sham tDCS + rest group). The 6-week intervention program was implemented with biweekly sessions, totaling 12 treatment sessions, each separated by a minimum 48-hour interval. After the tDCS intervention, the ST groups performed squat exercises while the tDCS + rest and sham tDCS + rest groups sat quietly for 30 minutes. Lower-limb maximal muscle strength was measured at 4 distinct time points: preintervention (T0), 24 hours post-third week intervention (T1), 24 hours post-sixth week final session (T2), and 1 week post-entire intervention completion (T3). Key evaluation metrics were measured, including 1 repetition maximum (1RM) squat, knee extensor and flexor peak torque, and rectus femoris cross-sectional area (CSA). Significant improvements in 1RM, knee extensor strength, and nondominant rectus femoris CSA were observed in both tDCS + ST and sham tDCS + ST groups compared with the sham tDCS-only group (p < 0.05). No differences in knee strength, 1RM, or rectus femoris CSA were observed between the tDCS + rest and sham tDCS + rest groups. The results indicate that anodal tDCS combined with ST does not yield additional training benefits on lower-limb maximal strength in healthy adults when compared with ST alone.

records.title: Do Athletes Lose Soleus Strength Over the Course of a Season? Longitudinal Monitoring of Seated Plantar Flexion Maximum Voluntary Contraction Strength and Factors That Affect It in Australian Football Players.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Do Athletes Lose Soleus Strength Over the Course of a Season? Longitudinal Monitoring of Seated Plantar Flexion Maximum Voluntary Contraction Strength and Factors That Affect It in Australian Football Players.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Green, B, Pizzari, T, Schache, AG, Rio, EK, Evans, SCS, Cooper, S, and Murphy, MC. Do athletes lose soleus strength over the course of a season? Longitudinal monitoring of seated plantar flexion maximum voluntary contraction strength and factors that affect it in Australian football players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The calf muscles are critical to dynamic lower-limb function in sports but are susceptible to injury. Despite its role in performance and injury, research has not evaluated soleus strength changes over the course of a season, or factors affecting it. Flexed-knee maximum plantar flexion strength was longitudinally monitored in state-league Australian footballers (2 Western Australian and 1 Victorian team) across 1-season at timepoints: preseason (T0), early in-season (T1), late in-season (T2). Generalized estimating equations evaluated strength outcomes over time (absolute, relative, asymmetry). Intrinsic factors (e.g., age, sex, injury history, sport exposure history, calf-focused resistance training) were analyzed to determine longitudinal associations with strength. Forty-one athletes (32 male, 9 female) were monitored across 210 strength measurements from T0 to T2. Absolute (T0 = 121.7 ± 27 kg; T1 = 135.2 ± 27.3 kg; T2 = 135.8 ± 25.9 kg) and relative (T0 = 1.51 ± 0.28 body mass [BM]; T1 = 1.69 ± 0.27 BM, T2 = 1.75 ± 0.26 BM) strength demonstrated longitudinal change (absolute: β = 19.33 kg, relative: β = 0.24 BM; p < 0.001). Reduced strength was associated with a recent calf injury history (relative and absolute: p < 0.001) and older age (p = 0.03). Lower strength (absolute: β = -23.53 kg, relative: β = -0.22 BM; p < 0.05) and larger asymmetry (β = 8.13 kg, p = 0.01) were detected in female athletes. Athletes can be expected to improve and maintain soleus capacity across seasonal periods. Athlete age, calf injury history, and sex can affect strength longitudinally. These findings may guide individualized prevention, performance, and postinjury benchmarking.

records.title: An Automated Blood Flow Restriction Device Is Reliable, but Not Valid, for Determining Lower Limb Occlusion Pressure in Resistance-trained Adults.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: An Automated Blood Flow Restriction Device Is Reliable, but Not Valid, for Determining Lower Limb Occlusion Pressure in Resistance-trained Adults.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Lang, D, Fallo, X, and Bennett, H. An automated blood flow restriction device is reliable, but not valid, for determining lower limb occlusion pressure in resistance-trained adults. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Blood flow restriction (BFR) exercise can improve strength, hypertrophy, and aerobic performance. Accurate limb occlusion pressure (LOP) assessment is essential for safe prescription. The AirBands is a novel automated BFR device that estimates LOP using integrated sensors, making LOP assessment easier. However, its validity and reliability are not well established in resistance-trained individuals. This study evaluated the concurrent validity of the AirBands compared with a handheld Doppler ultrasound for lower limb LOP, and its test-retest reliability, in resistance-trained adults. Twenty-six resistance-trained adults (14 males, 12 females; 24.2 ± 4.7 years) participated. For validity, LOP was measured using AirBands and Doppler in randomized order, using the same cuff. For reliability, automated LOP was measured twice, 10 minutes apart. Agreement was assessed using Bland-Altman limits of agreement and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC). No significant difference was observed between manual (231.7 ± 17.8 mm Hg) and automated (230.8 ± 38.3 mm Hg) LOP (mean difference -0.8 mm Hg; p = 0.928), although validity ICC was poor (0.236, 95% confidence interval [CI] = -0.293 to 0.641). Bland-Altman analysis indicated proportional bias, with overestimation at lower values and underestimation at higher values. Reliability showed no significant difference between test 1 (243.0 ± 37.5 mm Hg) and test 2 (242.3 ± 40.5 mm Hg) (mean difference 1.0 mm Hg; p = 0.816) and good reliability (ICC = 0.862, 95% CI = 0.715 to 0.936). AirBands demonstrates good test-retest reliability but poor concurrent validity vs. Doppler ultrasound. Clinicians should confirm automated values using a Doppler ultrasound before prescribing BFR.

records.title: Independent and joint associations of physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep with vitamin D status in US adults: a cross-sectional NHANES study.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Independent and joint associations of physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep with vitamin D status in US adults: a cross-sectional NHANES study.
content.abstract:
Background

Emerging evidence links movement behaviors to vitamin D status. This study investigated associations between physical activity (PA), sedentary behavior (SB), and sleep with vitamin D status and explored sex differences in these relationships.

Methods

This cross-sectional study included 3195 adults (49.1 ± 17.1 years, 45.5% males) from the 2021-2023 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey with complete data. Self-reported PA, SB, and sleep duration were assessed. Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D was measured using high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Generalized linear and logistic regression models were performed.

Results

SB was negatively associated with vitamin D levels in the whole sample (β = -0.006; 95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.012, -0.001) and males (β = -0.008; 95% CI: -0.014, -0.002), but not females. Sleep duration was positively associated with vitamin D among males only (β = 0.023; 95% CI: 0.003, 0.043). Meeting both PA and SB guidelines showed the strongest and most consistent association with vitamin D sufficiency, observed across the whole sample (odds ratio [OR] = 2.129; 95% CI: 1.504, 3.012), males (OR = 2.013; 95% CI: 1.021, 3.967), and females (OR = 2.214; 95% CI: 1.360, 3.605).

Conclusions

Movement behaviors demonstrate independent and joint associations with vitamin D status in US adults, with modest sex-specific patterns that warrant replication. Combined adherence to PA and SB guidelines was consistently associated with greater odds of vitamin D sufficiency across sexes.

records.title: Effects of milk fat globule membrane supplementation on physical function and body composition in older adults: a narrative review.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Effects of milk fat globule membrane supplementation on physical function and body composition in older adults: a narrative review.
content.abstract:
Background

Healthy aging is a priority for many individuals; however, a decline in physical function and poor body composition are common age-related changes that can cause the added years from rising life expectancy to be spent in poor health. Consequently, understanding the mechanisms involved in aging has become increasingly important, including the role of phospholipids (PLs) and how age-related changes in PL content may interfere with lipid metabolism and normal functioning of the musculoskeletal system. Milk fat globule membrane (MFGM) is a bovine milk fraction rich in PLs that may have the potential to support good physical health, so that quality of life can rise alongside life expectancy.

Methods

This narrative review was based on a literature search conducted on Google Scholar, PubMed, and Scopus in May 2026 using the following keywords and Boolean operators: milk fat globule membrane OR MFGM AND physical function OR body composition OR older adults. Studies were included if they were randomized clinical trials (RCTs) investigating MFGM's effects on physical function and/or body composition in older adults.

Results

Findings suggest that MFGM supplementation, when consumed in conjunction with exercise, is an effective way to improve physical function in older adults, particularly among Japanese cohorts; however, changes in habitual diet in response to exercise, variable PL concentrations, and other added ingredients used in interventions may have influenced these results.
